Segment names follow Oracle's fiscal 2025 presentation; from fiscal 2026 Oracle regrouped its reporting into Cloud, Software, Hardware and Services.

otherDetail: Interest expense of $842M on Oracle's debt pile, partly offset by $20M of other non-operating income, net.

segments.name: Cloud services & license support
segments.note: Renting Oracle's cloud, plus support for the software customers already run — the steady base of the business, 79% of all revenue.

segments.name: Cloud license & on-premise license
segments.note: New software licenses sold outright, for customers running Oracle on their own machines.

segments.name: Services
segments.note: Consulting and support services that help customers run Oracle products.

takeaways.text: Remaining performance obligations — work customers have signed for but Oracle has not yet delivered — reached a record $99B, up 53% from a year ago. Oracle also signed 42 new cloud GPU contracts worth $3B in the quarter as AI customers booked data-center capacity ahead.
takeaways.title: The backlog jumped 53%

takeaways.text: Cloud revenue — infrastructure plus applications — rose 21% to $5.6B, with cloud infrastructure alone up 45% to $2.2B and cloud applications up 10% to $3.5B. Hardware and services both shrank, so the mix keeps shifting toward recurring cloud rent.
takeaways.title: Cloud is carrying the growth

takeaways.text: Oracle paid $842M of interest in a single quarter on debt taken on to build data centers and buy back stock. Profit still rose 21%, but interest now eats about a fifth of operating income.
takeaways.title: Debt is the quiet cost

verdict: Oracle's revenue rose 7% to $13.3B as cloud revenue jumped 21% to $5.6B — and it kept $2.9B as profit, while its backlog of signed contracts surged 53% to a record $99B.
